verdicts.why: Four of the six sentences (a truth universally acknowledged, to own the truth, ignorant of the truth, a suspicion of the truth) use truth as the fact of the matter, which is the first-listed gloss; 'speaking the truth' is the true-statement sense and 'in truth' is a fixed adverbial, so the sentences split only at the edges and the first sense is the majority.

senses.why: The learner line restates 'a fact that has been verified' in plainer words, the opening-line example uses truth as a fact everyone accepts, no labels are claimed, and truth in this sense names a state of affairs without judging it, so null holds.

'Something said that is true' is the gloss 'a true statement' in plain words; both examples ('speaking the truth', 'a few plain truths') use the headword as a statement that is true, no labels are claimed, and the word describes without judging.

'The state of agreeing with what is really so' matches 'conformity to reality or actuality'; the philosophers' example uses truth as the abstract quality rather than a particular fact or statement, no labels are claimed, and the word in this sense carries no judgment of its referent.
